2. The second show cause notice was served upon the respondent on 13-3-73 proposing a penalty of dismissal. On 13-4-73, the respondent received a notice from the First Screening Board of the Government of Bangladesh charging him under Articles 5(A) and 5(I) of the Government of Bangladesh (Services Screening) Order, 1972, President's Order No. 67 of 1972. The respondent appearing before the Screening Board on 8-5-73 denied the charges of corruption and misconduct. Thereafter the respondent received an order of dismissal dated 31-5-73 from service of the Corporation with immediate effect. 

 3. It appears that the order of dismissal was passed pursuant to the decision of Board of Directors and in consideration of the recommendations of the First Screening Board constituted by the Government. The learned Judges of the High Court Division on consideration of the affidavits declared the impugned order dated 11-5-1973 dismissing the respondent from the service of the Corporation to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 7. Mr. Attorney-General has referred to a text book entitled Government Enterprise, Comparative Study, edited by W. Friedmann and J. F. Garner and has cited the passage: 

 The most likely field for State enterprise in an expanding economy is where private enterprise is undeveloped : in new industries and new products where the risks are great and the private entrepreneur—in an age of capital scarcity and high taxation of profits —may well hang back. This is no doubt one of the major motives for establishing a public corporation, and other forms of Government enterprise. The variety of forms in which the various States have, at different times, proceeded to establish public enterprises is almost infinite, but three main types emerge to which almost every public enterprise approximates: (1) departmental administration ; (2) the joint stock company controlled completely or partly by public authority; and finally (3) the public corporation proper, as a distinct type of corporation different from the private law company It appears to be a, universal practice that public corporations are created either by special statute or by a Government Ordinance. Unlike the commercial company they do not automatically come into existence by fulfilling certain statutory requirements. The creation of a public undertaking by special statute serves to distinguish the public corporation proper from the public undertaking which is established under the company law though the State provides the entire capital and holds all or virtually all the shares directly or through one of its own undertakings. The public corporations in the common law jurisdictions have entirely followed the rule that their employees should not have the status of civil servants. This is an outcome of the conception that the corporations should, as far as possible, approximate to the ideas of business management and not to be tied too closely to the civil service. But, there seems no present intention of changing this status. Nevertheless, service in the public corporations is not the same as service in a commercial company. It is a form of public service." 

 "The main disadvantages in departmentally run enterprises are rigidity of procedures, red tape and delay in taking and implementing decisions. All this arises because government procedures are applied to departmental enterprises and the proverbial red tape comes into vogue even in such cases which may not be conducive to the efficient management of a commercial enterprise. The staff of a departmental enterprise consists of civil servants whose terms of recruitment and conditions of service are the same as those of the other government servants. It is thus not possible to promote any one on merit or take prompt disciplinary action against any one when necessary. All these rigid procedures do not accord with accepted commercial or trading norms. These hamper individual judgment and initiative and taking of quick decisions which are necessary for the successful operation of a business enterprises. Thus departmental form of running commercial enterprise is, therefore, regarded as unsuitable. It has become necessary to use the technique of establishing autonomous bodies to run a business on behalf of the Government so as to give it commercial freedom. The system has grown because of the need to ensure freedom and flexibility of approach for an undertaking so that it may act with necessary expedition and initiative. A government company has most of the features of a private limited company and can function with the same initiative and freedom. Its employees are not civil servants. It can have its own rules of recruitment, promotion and dismissal of its employees. It is generally exempt from the budget accounting and audit procedures applicable to government departments. These advantages are ensured in case of a public corporation as well. The usual pattern of managing the affairs of a public undertaking is to have an apex body, a governing board, for the purpose. In case of government companies such boards are known as boards of directors and resemble similar boards in other private companies The position is now well established that the entity of government companies and statutory corporations is distinct and separate from the government and, therefore, the employees of a public undertaking are not regarded as civil servants and the protection of article 311 of the Constitution does not extend to them. (Vide Mafatlal Vs. Divisional Controller State Transport Corporation in A.I.R. 1966 S C. 1964). It has also been held that section 50 of the D. V. C. Act, 1948 which provides that the employees of the Corporation "shall be deemed., when acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the 'Act, to Fe-public servants within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code" would not bring the servants of a statutory corporation concerned within the fold of Article 311 of the Constitution of India. In that context we are also of the view that section 41(A) of the Act having similar provision as in section 50 of the D. V. C. Act cannot bring the respondent within the meaning of public servant. It has been held in the case of Rajasthan State Electricity Board, Jaipur Vs. Mohan Lal and others reported in A. I. R. 1967 S.C. 1857 that the Board as a statutory body comes within the purview of other authority under Article 12 of the Constitution of India and as such, such right can be enforced against it by a person affected." 

 In recent years a new class of corporations, has come into prominence. Corporations of this class are corporations aggregate, are created by Act of Parliament or by charter for the benefit or service of the community and are not, or are not now, owned by private individuals. Those corporations are here described as national corporations so as to limit the class to those corporations whose activities are not less than nation wise, but so as to include corporations which are part of a group having such activities, and so as to exclude, for example, development corporations for new towns whose purposes are local but which in many respects are similar corporations. "National corporations are public service corporations and carry on their undertakings as responsible independent corporations, not as part of any department of State. They may, however, be concerned with the execution of policy of the Government within the field of their activities, as for example, in the case of monetary policy, is the Bank of England, but in matters of routine, in the ordinary running of their undertakings and in the decisions necessary for that purpose, they act independently of the Government. They are usually subject, nevertheless, in some measure to the control of a department of State for which a Minister or other member of the Cabinet is responsible to Parliament, who commonly appoints the members of the national corporations and has the power to give it directions." 

 11. Study of techniques adopted by the Government indicates that one of the methods applied is to set up corporations. Broadly speaking they are called public corporations in contradistinction with private corporations set up under Companies Act by the citizens. The State policy is to utilise the principle of corporation. A corporation has its own independent existence distinct from the share holders or directors or administrators and has all the attributes of a juristic personality. A statutory corporation therefore is neither a dependent on Government nor its Agent unless there is something expressly contrary in the statute vide Tamlin Vs. Hannaford 1950(i) K. B. 18. 

 12. Public Corporations set up by the State again may assume various forms. It may choose to set up a corporation under the Companies Act either contributing entire share capital by the Government or dividing the contribution of share capital between the Government and the public. It may set up a Corporation by a statute This statutory corporation again is sometimes made amenable to different provisions of the Companies Act subject to the statute and sometimes it is kept totally outside the ambit of operation of the Companies Act, governable wholly by the incorporating statute itself. A public corporation may function as a Government department or its agent or both or may be totally independent of either having its own independent corporate personality. 

 13. We therefore find that a public corporation is a hybrid organism showing some of the features of a Government Department and some of a business company and standing outside the ordinary framework of Central and Local Government. As an administrative device it has been used for very long years but it has in particular come into prominence after independence from the British rules and also liberation of Bangladesh. Its purpose is to enable some industries or social service body to run for the benefit of the public but without the constraint of the parliamentary investigation and criticism to which it would be subject to if it were merely a Government Department, like the Post Office. In the case of an industry it must be master in its own house and there must be enough independence to encourage bold and farsighted decisions, subject only to the public interest. Thus there is a distinction between broad policy and day-to-day administration, the former being the sphere of the Government (and therefore the parliament) and the latter being the sphere of independent self management. In the case of social service, there must be devolution of responsibility so that there may be sonic degree of local independence with the necessary central control. The principle of corporation offers scope for many kinds of governmental experiment under which central control, local control and total independence can be blended in desired proportions. 

 15. Before dealing with the arguments of Mr. Attorney-General on the question of applicability of the master and servant rule to the employee of a Statutory Corporation, let us first dispose of the point urged at the bar as to whether such employees are entitled to the constitutional guarantee, as incorporated in Article 135 of the Constitution. it has been strenuously urged that various Presidential Orders and enactments such as President's Order No. 9 of 1972, President's Order No. 14 of 1972, President's Order No. 67 of 1972, President's Order No. 93 of 1972, Act 12 of 1974 and Act 38 of 1974, have clothed such employees with the status of 'Government Servants or 'Public Servants' and that such a status perforce entitles them to the benefit of the said constitutional guarantee. It should however be observed that the status of a Public Servant or a Government Servant has not been conferred generally upon an employee of a Statutory Corporation by the said Acts or Presidential Orders but have been so done for the purposes of the particular enactments. It has been made clear in the definition clause itself in each of these enactments, by prefacing the definition clause with the words, "In this Order" or "In this Act", as the case may be. Such definitions cannot therefore be read into the provisions of the Constitution and the status of a Government or Public Servant be attributed to the employees of a Statutory Corporation for the purpose of the constitutional provision of Article 135. This is also in accord with the well recognised rule of construction of a statute. 

 16. It would, however, be noticed that there is no reference to 'Government Servant' or 'Public Servant' in Article 135. It is a person. holding a civil post in the service of the Republic who is entitled to the protection provided in the said Article, and 'the service of the Republic has been defined in Article 152 of the Constitution as "any service, post or office, whether in a civil or military capacity, in respect of the Government of Bangladesh, and any other service declared by law to be a service of the Republic'. Article 135 contemplates, therefore, such service, post or office as is concerned with the governance or administration of Bangladesh as a State, and employees of Statutory Corporations which are set up by a modern State to carry out certain objects outside its traditional administrative responsibility can hardly come within the scope of the said definition. It is to be noted that the Acts or President's Orders to which reference has been made have scrupulously avoided any declaration of the service under a Statutory Corporation as a service of the Republic. 

 19. According to the English practice, however, the nature of the public character of a corporation is not determined by the nature of its origin and the policy of the law, but by the nature or purpose of its business. When a corporation is invested with some portion of the sovereign functions of the Government which is to be exercised by the corporation for the benefit of the public such a corporation may be said to have a public character, but a corporation, which, though instituted under a law of the country, is a body of certain individuals organised for the purpose of private benefits cannot be said to possess a public character. In a public corporation, very often the ultimate control is in the hands of the Government. 

 24. These principles as have been referred to above, have been by and large, incorporated in the law of judicial review as contained in Article 102(2) of the Constitution. This constitution power of a superior court can be invoked and the necessary direction or declaration can be given or made only against a person performing functions in connection with the affair of the Republic or of a local authority. The public character of the functionary against whom the necessary relief can be given under the constitutional power is manifest from the terms of the constitutional provision itself, as it requires that such functionary must be acting in the discharge of some public duties relating to the affairs of the State. The term local authority has not been defined in the Constitution but according to the definition as given in section 3(31) of the General Clauses Act it is clear that such term implies a public duty authorised by law or by the Government to carry on some administrative functions. A public corporation, as we have already noticed, is entrusted with some portion of the sovereign function of the Government which is to be performed by the Corporation for the benefit of the public and such a corporation is undoubtedly a person performing functions in relation to the affairs of the Republic within the meaning of Article 102(2) of the Constitution. What-ever uncertainty there might have been in regard to such an interpretation has now been removed by an amendment of the definition clause to the effect that a local authority includes a statutory body. Once it is accepted that an appropriate order under Article 102(2) of the Constitution may be made against a public corporation the court may make an order restraining it from doing what is not permitted by law to do or directing it to do what it is required by law to do or declaring that an act done or a proceeding taken by a public corporation has been done or taken without any lawful authority. Dismissal of an employee of such a corporation in violation of statutory rules or regulations is actionable for the purpose of restoration to office according to the constitutional mandate. Dismissal of an employee in violation of the principle of natural justice is also actionable in a similar way as the principle of natural justice must be regarded as a part of the statute, unless it is excluded therefrom by specific words. 

 28. The next important English case which has been cited before us is Barbar Vs. Manchester Regional Hospital Board and another 1958 1 All. E.R. 322 decided by the Queen's Bench Division. Barbar was employed as a consultant at a hospital administered by a local authority subject to the terms and conditions stated in a Memorandum issued by the Minister and it was held in the said case that the breach of clause 16 of the terms contained in the said Memorandum was nothing more than a breach of a contract between a master and a servant. The facts were that consequent on the establishment of the National Health Service on July 5, 1948, Manchester Regional Hospital Board, a regional hospital board, offered by a circular letter dated July 1, 1949 to continue the appointment among other persons of the plain-tiff, Barber who at the time was employed as a consultant at a hospital administered by a local authority, which, thereafter, came under the administration of the Board on behalf of Minister of Health. The continuance of Barber's employment was subject to the terms and conditions of the service of medical staff stated in a Memorandum of June, 1949, issued by the Minister. By clause 16 of those terms, the consultant, who considered that his appointment was being unfairly terminated by a Regional Hospital Board, was entitled to send a full statement of the facts to the Minister, who was then to place the case before a professional committee for their advice, in the light of which he would decide whether to confirm the termination of service, or to direct reinstatement, or to arrange some third solution agreeable to the parties concerned. This proceeding was to be completed before a Board's decision to terminate a consultant's service was carried into effect. The plaintiff Barber continued in the employment of the Board as Hospital consultant. In January 1952, the Board purported to terminate the plaintiff's employment as from April 30, 1952 and the plaintiff considering his dismissal unfair, caused, the Minister to be informed of the facts, but it was maintained on behalf of the Minister that no appeal lay to him, and the Minister, therefore, reached no decision under clause 16. The plaintiff brought an action against the Board and the Minister, claiming declaration that his employment with the Board was subject to the terms and conditions of service issued by the Minister and that it was never validly deter-mined. He also claimed damages for breach of contract for wrongful dismissal and, as against the Minister, a declaration that in failing to comply with clause 16, the Minister acted in breach of his statutory duty under the National Health Service Act, 1964. Distinguishing the case of Vine Vs. National Dock Labour Board (1956) 3 All. E.R. 939, it was held by the Queen's Bench Judge that the contract of Barber with the Board was one between Master and Servant, the termination of which could not be a nullity, and the plaintiff was not, therefore, entitled to a declaration that his employment had never been validly determined, but was entitled only to recover damages for breah of contract. The case of Vine Vs. National Dock Labur Board was distinguished in this case in the following manner: 

 31. In Vidyodaya University of Ceylon and others Vs. Silva 1964 (3) All E. R. (P. C.) 865, the facts were that by Statute establishing and regulating Vidyodaya University of Ceylon, the University by its executive body the University Council were empowered to institute professorship, and every appointment of professor was to be by agreement in writing between the University and the Professor, and was to be for such period and for such terms as the Council might resolve. By s. 18(e) of the Act of 1958 the Council had power to dismiss any officer or teacher on grounds of incapacity or conduct which in the opinion of not less than two third members of the Council, renders him unfit to be an officer or teacher of the University. The Act of 1958 did not expressly give a right of hearing, nor provide any right of appeal. The term 'Officer' included the Vice-Chancellor and the holder of any other office created by statute, and the terms 'teacher' included a professor, lecturer or other person imparting instruction. By letter dated September 1, 1960, the respondent pursuant to the Council's decision, was appointed professor and Head of the Department of Economics and Business Administration at the University, and by letter dated September 2, 1960, he accepted the appointment. He did not sign the form of agreement for use on the appointment of teacher in the University. by letter dated July 4, 1961 the respondent was informed by the Vice-Chancellor that at a meeting of the Council held that day, it had been unanimously resolved to terminate his appointment from that day. The respondent sought a writ certiorari to quash the Council's order dismissing him, on the ground that the Council were bound to act judicially in terminating his appointment and should therefore, have told him of the nature of the accusation and given him an opportunity of being heard. The Ceylon Supreme Court granted certiorari. On appeal to the Privy Council, the Board considered Vine's case among other authorities, and held that, although, the University was established and regulated by statute that did not make the contract of employment made with the teachers and subject to. S. 18(a), it Was no other than ordinary contract between master and servant; and in the present case the respondent was not shown to have any status other than that of a servant, and that the procedure by certiorari was not available where master summarily terminated servant's employment. It was held that certiorari had been wrongly granted. 

 33. It may also be pointed out, with respect, that the case of Vidyodaya University also, appears to be of doubtful validity, as it is not consistent with well known judicial principle and some distinguished English judicial authorities. There also the employment of the respondent as the Professor and Head of the Department of Economics and Business Administration of the University was taken to be a contractual one in view of the fact that the execution of a deed of permanent contract was contemplated. Under section 18(a) of the Act of 1958 under which the University was established the University Council had power to dismiss an officer or a teacher on grounds of incapacity or conduct which in the opinion of not less than two-third members of the Council render him unfit to be an officer or a teacher and under the said provision the respondent was dismissed by the Council without being given any opportunity of being heard. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council treated it to be a case of pure master and servant and as such the respondent was held to be not entitled to any declaration as to the invalidity of the order of dismissal. The decision of this case runs counter to the well established principle recognised in English Courts that any person being empowered under law to determine questions affecting the right of another person is bound to exercise that power judicially and observe the principle of natural justice. 

 35. In 1956 the appellant Ridge was appointed Chief Constable of Borough Police Force, the appointment being subject to the Police Acts and Regulations. On October 25, 1957 he was arrested and charged, together with other persons, with conspiracy to obstruct the course of justice, On October 28, 1957, he was suspended from duty by the Borough Watch Committee. On February 28, 1958, he was acquitted by the jury on the criminal charges against him, but Donovan J. in passing sentence on two police officers who were convicted, said that the facts admitted in the course of the trial "establish that neither of you had that professional and moral leadership which both of you should have had and were entitled to expect from the Chief Constable'. On March 6, 1958, on a charge alleging corruption against the appellant, on which no evidence was offered, the judgment referred to the borough's police force and remarked on its need for a leader "who will be a new influence and who will set a different example from that which has lately obtained". After his acquittal the appellant applied to be re-instated, but on March 7, 1958, the Watch Committee at a meeting decided that he had been negligent in the discharge of his duties as Chief Constable and, in purported exercise of the powers conferred on them by section 191(4) of the Act of 1882, dismissed him from that office. No specific charge was formulated against him either at that meeting or at another on March 18, when the appellant's solicitor addressed the Committee, but the Watch Committee, in arriving at their decision, considered (inter alia) his own statements in evidence and the observations made by Donvan J. on February 28 and March 6. On the appellant's appeal to the Home Secretary, the decision given was "that there was sufficient material on which the Watch Committee could properly exercise their power of dismissal under section 191(4)." The appellant then brought an action against members of the Watch Committee for a declaration that his dismissal was illegal, ultra vires and void, and payment of salary from March 7, 1958, or alternatively, payment of pension from that date and damages. It was held that the decision of the respondents to dismiss the appellant was null and void; and that, accordingly, notwithstanding that the decision of the Home Secretary was "final and binding on the parties" by section 2(3) of the Police Appeals Act, 1927, that decision could not give validity to the decision of the respondents. The decision of the respondents was a nullity. 

 "In my judgment once there was a report or allegation from which it appeared that a Chief Constable might have committed an offence, it was a condition precedent to any dismissal based on a finding of guilt of such offence that the Regulations should in essentials have been put into operation. They included and incorporated the principles of natural justice which, as Haman L. J. (1962 (1) All. E. R. at p. 850) said, only fair play in action. It is well established that the essential requirements on natural justice at least include that before someone is condemned he is to have an opportunity of defending himself and that in order that he may do so he is to be made aware of the charges of allegations or suggestions which he has to meet: See Kanada Vs. Government of Federation of Malaya. (1962 A. C. 322). My Lords, here is something which is basic to our system; the importance of upholding it far transcends the significance of any particular case." 

 "The argument that once it is shown that the relevant relationship is that of master and servant, this is sufficient to exclude the requirements of natural justice is often found, in one form or another, in reported cases. There are two reasons behind it. The first is that, in master and servant cases, one is normally in the field of the i common law of contract inter parties, so that principles of administrative law, including those of natural justice, have no part to play, The second relates to the remedy : it is that in pure master and servant cases, the most that can be obtained is damages, if the dismissal is wrongful; no order for reinstatement can be made, so no room exists for such remedies as administrative law may grant, such as a declaration that the dismissal is void. I think, there is validity in both of these arguments, but they, particularly the first, must be carefully used. It involves the risk of compartmental approach which, although convenient as a solvent, may lead to narrower distinctions than are appropriate to the broader issues of administrative law. A comparative list of the situations in which persons have been held entitled or not entitled to a hearing or to observation of rules of natural justice, according to the master and servant test, looks illogical and even bizzarre. A specialist surgeon is denied protection which is given to a hospital doctor; a University professor, as a servant, has been denied the right to be heard, a dock labourer and an undergraduate have been granted it; example's can be multiplied (See Barber Vs. Manchester Regional Hospital Board (1958 1 All. E. R. 322, Palmer Vs. Inverness Hospitals Board (1963 SC 311), Vidyodaya University of Ceylon Vs. Silva, (1964) 3 All. E. R. 65, Vine Vs. National Dock Labour Board, (1957 A. C. 488), Glynn Vs. Keele University, (1971) 1 W.L.R. 487. One may accept that if there are relationships in which all requirements of the observance of rules of natural justice are excluded (and I do not wish to assume that this is inevitably so) these must be confined to what have been called pure master and servant cases, which I take to mean cases in which there is no element of public employment or service, no support by statute, nothing in the nature of an office or a status which is capable of protection. If any of these elements exist, then in my opinion whatever the terminology used, even though in some inter parties aspects the relationship may be called that of master and servant, there may be essential procedural requirements to be observed, and failure to observe them may result in a dismissal being declared to be void. 

 49. The learned Judges—they were two, Shelat and Vaidialingam, JJ—appear to have taken the view that the Regulations framed by the Corporation have no statutory force and a breach of the same does not entitle the employee to a declaration of the order made in contravention thereof to be a nullity on the reasoning that the Act does not guarantee any statutory status to the employee nor does it impose any obligation on the Corporation in such matters. Reference was made in course of the judgment to only three Indian decisions, namely, Dr. S. Dutt Vs. University of Delhi, A.I.R. 1958 S. C. 1050, S.R. Tewari Vs. District Board, Agra, A.I.R. 1964. S C. 1680, and Life Insurance Corporation of India Vs. Sunil Kumar Mukherjce, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 849 none of which dealt with the specific point on which the aforesaid view was expressed. But this view appears to have been further developed and more elaborately discussed in the subsequent case of Indian Airlines Corporation Vs. Sukhedo which was heard by a Bench of three Judges, viz. Shelat, Duo and Bhargava, JJ. 

 At another place of the judgment there is a reference to the aforesaid case of Ram Babu Rathaur, where it has been observed that there having been no statutory obligation imposed upon the Corporation, the High Court was right in holding in the said case that the general law of master and servant would apply. This observation appears to have been made on the assumption, as was found by the High Court, that there was no statutory provision regulating the conditions of service in the said case, without applying its mind to the question as to whether the said finding of the High Court was well reasoned or justified. The Supreme Court decision on the other hand proceeded to examine the facts of the case on the view that the Rule 3A framed by the State Government under section 172(2) of the District Boards Act, 1922 laying down the conditions under which the service of a permanent servant of the Board could be terminated had statutory force and required to be complied with, and ultimately disposed of the appeal by holding that the order of termination of service was lawful as the provision of Rule 3A was duly complied with. 

 54. In the said two Privy Council cases, the Judicial Committee had to consider the case of two crown servants dismissed in violation of Statutory rules and held, on the construction of section 76-B of the Government of India Act, 1919 that the service of a crown servant being at the pleasure of the sovereign and having regard to the specific provision in the said section providing that no rules or other provisions made thereunder should be construed to limit or abridge the power of the Secretary of State to deal with a civil servant, any breach of such statutory rules was not actionable in a court of law. It should be noticed that their Lordships of the Judicial Committee were not laying down a general proposition applicable to all cases of employer and employee, but they were considering the specific position of crown servants under section 76B of the Government of India Act, 1919. We do not see how these decisions could be brought in aid of the case of an employee of a Statutory Corporation. 

 57. In Kruse Vs. Johnson, the validity of a bye-law, made by a County Council under a certain provision of the Local Government Act, 1888 was challenged on the ground of unreasonableness, and it was held that the bye-law in question was not bad for unreasonableness. The ground of challenge in this case appears to be novel, no doubt, as seldom a legislative enactment can be thrown out on the ground of unreasonableness, if legislative competence is there. But in case of a delegated legislation, as the said case was, the question becomes relevant in judging whether the body exercising delegated authority framed the impugned bye-law within the limits of its delegated power, as the legislature cannot be Presumed to have delegated any authority to make an unreasonable provision. It is really a question relating to ultra vires, which may be pertinent in regard to the exercise of the power of subordinate legislation. 

 59. In the case of Life Insurance Corporation of India and others Vs. Sunil Kumar Mukherjee and others reported in A.I.R. 1964. S. C. 849, the Supreme Court of India had to examine the validity and comparative efficacy of different kinds of subordinate legislations. Udder the Life Insurance Corporation Act, the employee's of various Insurance Companies became the employees of the newly set up Corporation on the same terms and conditions as they had as employees under the said Companies unless and until their employments were terminated or until their terms and conditions were duly altered by the Corporation. Government issued an Order under section 11 of the Act, clause (10) of which provided that in case of unsatisfactory performance, misconduct, negligence etc. the service of an employee might be terminated after giving him an opportunity of showing cause against action proposed to be taken against him. Under section 49 of the Act the Corporation had the power to frame Regulations, and one of clauses of the Regulations framed by the Corporation prescribed that in judging a Field Officer's work, the Corporation should observe the principle contained in the circular issued by the Managing Director and the said circular provided, inter aria, that in case poor performance etc. the services of the Field officers would be terminated. The Corporation terminated the services of the respondents by an order without giving them any prior notice, Respondents contention was that the order of termination was bad as they were not given any opportunity to show cause against the action taken against them, as was clearly provided in clause (10) of the Government Order made under section 11 of the Act. The Corporation's contention on the other hand was that under para 4(a) of the circular issued under clause (11) of the Government Order such kind of termination was provided. It was held in the said case that the procedure laid down in clause (10) of the Government Order could not be superseded by a circular issued under a Regulation framed under section 49 read with clause (11) of the Order and that as such the order of termination made in violation of the Government order was invalid. Gajendragadkar, J (as he then was), with whom Wanchoo and Das Gupta JJ concurred, in explaining the legal position about the character of the relevant statutory provisions made the following observation: 

 "It is plain that the provisions contained in section 11(2) of the Act are paramount and would over-ride any contrary provisions contained in the Order or Regulations. Subject to the provisions of section 11(2), the provisions of the Order will prevail, because the Order has been issued by the Central Government by virtue of the powers conferred on it by section 11(2) itself. The provisions of the Order in law partake of the character of the rules framed under section 48 of the Act. Thus next to the provisions of section 11(2) of the Act will stand the provisions of the Order. Then we have the Regulations issued by the Corporation under section 49(1) of the Act. But it must be borne in mind that the power of the Corporation to make the Regulations is burdened with the conditions that these regulations must not be inconsistent with the Act and the rules framed thereunder, so that if any of the provisions contained in the Regulations made by the Corporation under section 49 are found to be inconsistent either with section 11(2) or with the Order made by the Central Government under section 11(2) would be invalid. It is in the light of this legal position that the problem posed before us in the present appeals must be decided." 

 65. Reference was, of course, also made in both the later two decisions of the Indian Supreme Court to the case of Dr. S. Dutt Vs. University of 1958 S.C. 1050, where it was observed that when an award held that a Professor of the University had been dismissed wrongfully and malafide, that the dismissal had no effect on his status and that he still continued to be a Professor of the University, it directed specific enforcement of a contract of personal service and as such was clearly erroneous. This case assumed that there was no element involved in that case other than that of breach of a contract of personal service. As a matter of fact, in repelling a contention made on behalf of the appellant on the basis of the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case, The High Commissioner for India Vs. I.M. Dall 75 Ind. App. 225 same case A.I.R. 1948 P.C. 121, the learned Judges of the Supreme Court of India observed that all that the Judicial Committee did in that case was to make a declaration of a statutory invalidity of an act, which was a thing entirely different from enforcing a contract of personal service. This case, thus we see, had nothing to do with the character or import of a subordinate legislation like a Regulation. We must, however, observe, as it has occurred to us, that in the said case of the Delhi University the full attention of the Court was not paid to the other aspect of the matter to which we shall presently revert. The Single Judge decision of the Allahabad High Court is of course an exception, but we have already seen that the said decision is founded on a wrong premise. 

 73. The first important decision on the question is the case of Tariq Transport Company Vs. Sargodha:-Bhera Bus Service reported in 11 D.L.R. (S.C.) 140 same case P.L.D. 1958 S.C. Pak . 437, where Munir C.J. while examining the limits of judicial review of the administrative acts enunciated the rule in the following words: 

 76. In the case of Messrs Faridsons Ltd. Vs. Government of Pakistan, the Import Registration Certificates of the two appellants were suspended and one of the appellants was debarred from getting any Export Registration Certificate, by the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports without giving any opportunity of being heard. The West Pakistan High Court, Karachi Bench, dismissed the application of the appellants for a writ on the view that the Chief Controller was not required by law to act judicially and that the rule of natural justice which was based on certain English precedents had no application to Pakistan which was wholly governed by statute law. On appeal from the said decision, the Supreme Court of Pakistan reversed the said view and it was pointed out that in Mrs. Dina Sohrab Khatrak's case it had already been laid down by the Pakistan Supreme Court that the maxim, audi alteram partem 'No man shall be condemned unheard' applied to all judicial or administrative bodies, specially where the proceedings taken may affect the person or property or other rights of the parties concerned in the dispute. The Tariq Transport Company's case was distinguished on the footing that no private rights were involved in the matters coming up for decision before the Transport Authority which was to decide in accordance with what they conceived to be larger public interest. It was, however, noticed in the judgment of S.A. Rahman, J delivered in Messrs Faridsons Ltd.'s case that the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council expressed a view in Nakhuda Ali Vs. Jayratne (1951) A.C. 66 to the effect that it was not enough that a body should have legal authority to determine a question affecting the rights of the subject, but that there must be super added to it a duty `to act judicially' and the learned Judge appears to have clearly dissented from the said view of the Judicial Committee by observing that it "seems to run counter to a long line of English decision in the English Courts, extending back for more than a century, in "which administrative decisions affecting individuals rights and liberties were quashed if the party concerned had not been given a fair opportunity to make objection. We have already noted that the House of Lords expressed the same view in Ridge Vs. Baldwin as Mr. Justice S.A. Rahman in respect of the view of the Judicial Committee in Nakhuda Ali Vs. Jayratne. 

 84. In the case of Zainul Abedin Vs. Multan Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. Multan reported in 18 DLR (SC) 462 same case PLD 1966 SC 445, the Supreme Court of Pakistan took a view that for the purpose of restoration to office a writ of mandamus was not available to the appellant, who as an Accountant of the Co-operative Bank was dismissed from the service of the said Bank on the grounds of, inter-alia, want of necessary qualification and actions detrimental to the interest of the institution. An appeal was filed against the order of dismissal (as not being) in accordance with the Civil Service Rules as adopted by the respondent Bank, to the Commissioner of Development, who allowed the appeal on the view that no reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken was given to the employee concerned, as required under the Civil Service Rules, and set aside the order of the Registrar Co-operative Societies under whose directive the order of termination was issued by the Bank. This order was communicated to the Bank by the Commissioner, Co-operative Societies, West Pakistan, but the Bank having refused to implement the Government order and reinstate the appellant, the High Court was moved in its writ jurisdiction, but it rejected the appellant's application summarily. On appeal, the Supreme Court having held that there was no statutory duty cast upon the Bank requiring it to carry out the appellate orders of the Government made under the Act on the rules framed thereunder and that the office of an Accountant of a Co-operative Bank was not one of public nature, did not consider it a proper case where the writ of Mandamus should issue. It is not necessary for our present purpose to see whether the Supreme Court of Pakistan was correct in view that there was no statutory duty cast upon the Bank to comply with an order made by the Government under the Act or the rules framed thereunder or that the office of an Accountant of the Bank was not an office of public nature. It is sufficient for our purpose to notice that the Supreme Court accepted the principle that if the office from which an employee has been dismissed is of public nature, the limitation of the master and servant rule cannot be invoked. It also appears that the Supreme Court accepted the principle that a writ might issue if there was contravention of a statutory provision of a binding nature. 

 86. It is difficult to concur with the view as expressed in this judgment as to the character of the Corporation concerned, but no exception may perhaps be taken to the proposition of law which appears to have been laid down in the said case, namely, that the Court has power to issue a writ requiring restoration of a dismissed employee to an office of public nature. What office can be said to be of public nature does not appear to have been analysed and examined in any of the decisions of the Pakistan Supreme Court. In three of the earlier cases viz. The Lahore Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. Vs. Pir Saifullah Khan, Faiz Ahmed Vs. Registrar, Co-operative Societies Ltd. and Zainul Abedin Vs. Mutton CO-operative Bank Ltd, the Corporation concerned were co-operative Banks which, though subject to some kind of control of the Provincial Government through the Registrar Co-operative Societies, were not considered to have sufficient public character, whereas the Corporation concerned in the case of The Managing Committee of Co-operative Model Town Society Ltd. Vs. Khan Mohammad lqbal, though a co-operative society was considered to have some kind of public character. 

 87. If we examine the object, structure and mode of operation of East Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation, there is hardly any scope for doubt that it was a public corporation. It was set up under the Central Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1962 under the exclusive control of the Government for the purpose of promoting economic and industrial development of East Pakistan which was undoubtedly a public purpose. The general direction and administration of the Corporation and its affairs vested in a Board of Directors, all of whom were to be appointed by the Government and who were guided by such directions, as the Government might give it from time to time. The learned Judges deciding Rustom Ali's case themselves found that East Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation was a person within the meaning of Article 98(2) of the then Pakistan Constitution and such a finding at once established the public character of the Corporation, as such a Corporation could not be a person within the meaning of the said constitutional provision unless it performed functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority. As the specific character of the said Corporation was not closely examined and its distinguishing features from those of the institutions which are considered private, were noticed in Rustom Ali's case, the said decision is not at all helpful for the correct under-standing of the law on the subject. 

 92. We have already noticed that an employee of a statutory Corporation cannot claim the status of one in the service of the Republic, but the public character of such an employee has been recognised in a number of legislative enactments where such an employee has been given—although for the purposes of the said enactments—the status of a 'Government Servant' or a 'Public Servant'. A detailed examination of these legislative measures is not necessary except for the purpose of examining their bearing on the character of the Corporation. It appears that President's Order No. 25 of 1973 provides for recruitment of certain categories of officers of statutory corporations on the recommendations of the Public Service Commission set up under the Constitution. Furthermore, the General Clauses Act has now been amended and by an inclusive definition, all statutory corporations are now Local Authorities. Such a definition unmistakably underlines the public character of these Corporations. 

 95. We now turn to the merits of the appeal. The learned Attorney-General strenuously urged that the principle governing the relationship between Master and Servant would apply in the facts and accordingly he took us to the provisions of Bangladesh Small and Cottage Industries Corporation Act, 1957 (Act XVII of 1957), hereinafter referred to as the Act. Under Section 3(2) of the Act the appellant is a body corporate by the name of Small and Cottage Industries Corporation, subject to the provisions of the Act, to acquire and hold property, both moveable, and immoveable and shall by the said name sue and be sued. Under Section 4(3) of the Act the Bangladesh Government shall be a share-holder of the Corporation and shall subscribe to and hold not less than fifty-one per cent of the shares issued by the Corporation at any time; the remaining shares shall be reserved for public subscriptions. The management of the Corporation has been vested in a Board of Directors under Sections 6 and 7 of the Act consisting not more than five and all appointed by the Government. Under section 9(1) of the Act Bangladesh Government is required to appoint one of the Director of the Board who shall be the Chief Executive of the Corporation. Under section 13 of the Act, the Corporation may appoint or employ such persons as it considers necessary for the efficient performance of its functions. Section 45 of the Act provides for making rules by the Government not inconsistent with this Act for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of this Act and where the regulations framed under section 46 of the Act are inconsistent with the rules, the rules shall prevail. Under section 46(1) of the Act the Board may, with the previous sanction of the Government, make regulations not inconsistent with this Act or the rules made under this Act to provide for all matters for which provisions is necessary or expedient for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of this Act. Under section 46(2) (h) of the Act the Board has been empowered to make regulations for the terms and conditions of service, duties and conduct of officers, servants and agents of the Corporation. The regulations have been framed under section 46(2)(k) and the regulations so framed were published in the Extraordinary Dacca Gazette on 3rd May, 1965. 

 98. Bearing the principles adumbrated above, we find that majority of the shares is held by the Government but public subscription is also considerable. However, the management and control of the Corporation is vested in a Board of Directors, not exceeding five and all appointed by the Government. Though there is public subscription of shares, there is no public participation in the management and control of the Corporation. If we turn to the function and object of the Corporation, we observe that principal aim is to help promote small industries by giving loan, advice and sometime starting project and then selling it to prospective investors. The purpose is public service, it is promotional and for development for the benefit and service of the community, and not for any profitable commercial undertaking. The Corporation has a definite public service in view viz., to promote small industries and help their investors. It has therefore a public character. Its employees partake of that public Character. 

 99. Along with it is to be noted that by the provision of General Clauses Act, this statutory Corporation is deemed to be a local authority. Local authority connotes a kind of public administration. Again by various legislative measures set out above the employee of statutory corporations have sometimes been described as Government servants and some-times as public servants. No doubt each of this legislative enactments is limited to the purpose of its own, nonetheless it cannot be denied that the cumulative effect of these legislative measures have at least clothed them with some public character.
